newsitem.title: INDIA: India leaders try to break Chidambaram's silence.
newsitem.headline: India leaders try to break Chidambaram's silence.

text.p: Rival suitors were trying to lure Indian politician P. Chidambaram on Thursday, but the ex-finance minister maintained his silence on whether he and his regional party will formally rejoin the ruling coalition.

The presence of Chidambaram, who earned widespread respect for continuing bold economic reforms and drafting a landmark 1997/98 budget, would boost the political credibility of Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's United Front coalition.

But the Congress party, which gives make-or-break support to the coalition, is also wooing Chidambaram and his Tamil Maanila Congress (TMC), a regional party formed by Congress defectors from the southern state of Tamil Nadu.

Chidambaram and TMC leader G.K. Moopanar quit Congress last year over a disagreement and formed their own party, but Congress is eager to bring them back into the fold to boost its clout, and profile, in parliament.

On Sunday, the TMC announced it would remain a member of the 15-party ruling alliance but said it would not take a government role. It objected to Moopanar being passed over in the coalition's leadership tussle last week.

United News of India (UNI) on Thursday quoted TMC sources as saying the party's executive committee, due to meet on Sunday in Madras, was expected to reverse the party's decision to keep out of the government.
Chidambaram declined to comment on the issue.
"I am observing my vow of silence," he told Reuters by telephone. "I don't know when I will break it."
Gujral, who had appealed to Chidambaram to change his mind during a confidence vote which he won on Tuesday, said on Thursday he was hopeful the TMC would return to the government.
"I am trying," he told Asian News International television. "I am optimistic."
UNI, however, said there still were divisions within the TMC as some of its deputies wanted to stay out of the government while retaining membership in the United Front.

The Congress party triggered a politicial crisis last month when it withdrew its support for the United Front, prompting a confidence vote that former prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda lost but Gujral later won after Congress resumed its fickle backing.
Congress members are keen for Chidambaram and TMC members to return to the once powerful party, which, until 1996, had ruled India for all but four years since independence in 1947.
The TMC has 20 seats in the 542-member lower house of parliament. The alliance controls 178, including the TMC seats, while Congress controls 140.
Congress president Sitaram Kesri met Moopanar on Wednesday with a plea to return to his old party.

"The United Front has hurt the Tamil pride," a Congress official told Reuters, echoing the view expressed by some TMC deputies. "As far as our party stand is concerned we want all the former Congressmen to return to the fold."
Gujral, who has kept the finance ministry portfolio, is expecting Chidamabram to return to his old post before parliament reconvenes for the budget session on April 30.
On Thursday, Gujral's cabinet adopted the 1997/98 (April-March) budget which had been presented to parliament by Chidambaram in February.

An official spokesman told reporters the government looked forward to parliament adopting the budget, and would not discuss any amendments outside of parliament because the tax and spending plan was before lawmakers for their consideration.
